source.title: On the Multiple Descent of Minimum-Norm Interpolants and Restricted Lower Isometry of Kernels
source.authors: Tengyuan Liang; A. Rakhlin; Xi-Yu Zhai

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes minimum-norm interpolants in RKHS and reports theoretical risk bounds and empirical variance curves bearing on multiple descent, using a different model class and analysis from the original deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own risk bounds and its Figure 2 experiment. Results cited from other work are not recorded. Figure 2 varies dimension at fixed n=5000 and plots variance, not total test error from a sample-size sweep.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes minimum-norm RKHS (kernel ridgeless) interpolants with theory and one experiment. Figure 2, at n=5000, shows the variance has multiple peaks as d varies, at the theoretically predicted locations. That bears on the multiple-peaks part of V6 in a non-deep model class. Its other results are upper bounds, which cannot show actual risk rising.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors stress a positive message: the interpolant's risk provably vanishes in n for most scalings d≍n^α. The bounds also yield generalization guarantees for wide neural networks through the NTK. They say the multiple peaks generalize double descent, and that a lower bound and the effect of regularization on the peaks remain open.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes ridgeless kernel regression and kernel-related variance and risk bounds, rather than sweeping deep-network model size, training epochs, or sample size in the original experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Theoretical rates depend on the dimension/sample-size scaling and kernel assumptions; the empirical plot varies dimension at fixed sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: The risk upper bound has valleys at d=n^(1/(ι+1/2)) and becomes vacuous at α=1/i. The best attainable rate worsens as α approaches 0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For kernel ridgeless regression, the rate of the risk upper bound is non-monotone in the scaling exponent α, where d=n^α.

record.problems: The experiments are presented as a plot without numerical values in the text and show variance rather than total test error. The theoretical results are upper bounds; the authors state that a lower bound exhibiting multiple descent remains open.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for cited findings from prior work. The paper's other technical results do not separately report outcomes on the claim versions.

untested.parts: Deep-network model-size sweeps. The NTK corollary gives only upper-bound guarantees.
No measured test error as n grows at fixed d. The fixed-d reading comes from an upper bound only.
No sweep of capacity through an interpolation threshold. All estimators interpolate, and the axis is input dimension.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
No measured label-noise dependence. The effect of regularization on the peaks is named as future work.

missing.what: In the noiseless case the variance term is zero and the interpolant is consistent. Theoretically, this ties the peaks to label noise and variance.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The reader's V3 and V4 limits_scope labels rested on rows that cannot show the effect, so they are dropped. All V3 rows are upper bounds, so no V3 verdict is given. Figure 2 varies d at fixed n, not n. Tranche could also be read as T3, a new model-class setting.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model size and test error.
The experiment does not sweep sample size at fixed dimension or report total test error; the sample-size interpretation is of an upper bound.
The study does not sweep model capacity past an empirically identified interpolation point or measure total risk in its experiment.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
No systematic test of label-noise dependence, multiple peaks caused by noise or variance, or optimally tuned regularization. Regularization effects are named as future work.
No comparison against an effective parameter count or test of whether re-counting complexity makes descent U-shaped.

rows.subject: minimum-norm interpolant in RKHS
rows.operation_detail: Analyze an upper bound on out-of-sample risk for dimension and sample-size scalings d=n^α.

conditions.value: Conditions on f*, h and PX specified by Theorems 2–3

rows.measure: Conditional expected squared L2(PX) prediction error upper bound
rows.uncertainty: With probability at least 1−δ−e^(−n/d^ι) over the design
rows.note: The paper says the upper bound has valleys and, with fixed d, can have alternating better and worse regimes as n increases. It also states that the peaks and a lower bound for the multiple-descent behavior remain open; the bound does not establish that actual test error rises.
rows.check: This is an upper bound on risk. The authors say a matching lower bound is open, so it cannot show that test error actually rises with n. The informal theorem's 'Section 1' locator is correct.

rows.subject: minimum-norm interpolant in RKHS
rows.operation_detail: Plot the variance of the minimum-norm interpolant while varying input dimension.

conditions.value: Vertical lines denote theoretically predicted peaks

rows.note: The text says the experiment shows multiple peaks and that their locations align with predictions. The plot is of variance versus dimension at fixed sample size, not total test risk versus model capacity.
rows.check: Relink from V4 to V6. The figure shows multiple variance peaks versus log d at fixed n=5000, which is multiple descent. It is not a capacity sweep past an interpolation threshold, since every model interpolates, and it does not vary sample size, so it does not bear on V3. Per the text, the peaks 'confirm the surprising multiple-peaks behavior'. The y-axis is variance only, which the authors argue dominates the shape.
